0095.event: At Konso in Ethiopia, about one million four hundred thousand years ago, the ground is thick with handaxes, not by the dozen but by the thousand. This was a quarry-workshop, a place where good stone came out of the earth and many hands shaped it, feeding tools across the whole valley. The teardrops lie piled in every stage: rough beginnings, fine symmetrical blades, and the flakes struck off in between. No single maker could have done this alone. It was a people's work, the first industry, hands gathered to one purpose with dust in the air and the ring of stone on stone. The handaxe had become a common art, and the valley was its factory floor.
0095.announce: The valley rings with hammerstones, in verse: The Konso Workshops.
0095.title: The Konso Workshops
0095.piece:
Come to the quarry where the good stone lies.
Take up the hammer. Let the waste rock fly.
A thousand handaxes wait to be born.
We shape them from the early morn.
Strike, and turn, and strike again.
The teardrop grows beneath the strain.
Not one alone, but rank on rank,
the finest blades the valley's bank
of stone can give. We work as one.
The dust is thick. The day is long.
The ringing of the stone is our song.
Industry's first chorus, loud and strong.
Take up your hammer. Join the line.
This thousand blades, and all are mine,
and yours, and ours. The valley feeds
the hands that shape to meet its needs.

0096.event: In Kenya, about one million three hundred thousand years ago, stone tools lie scattered on both walls of the great Rift Valley, east and west alike. The bands moved freely across the whole valley, up the ridges and down into the dells, and no border stopped them. The same kinds of tools appear on every side, which says the same hands, or hands that learned from each other, walked everywhere. The crossroads was never marked with signs. It was written in the wear of a million crossing lines in the dust. Long before anyone drew a line on a map, the valley was one country, and feet were its only passport.
0096.announce: A crossroads ballad for the whole valley: The Rift Crossroads.
0096.title: The Rift Crossroads
0096.piece:
East wall, west wall, the tools lie free,
no border drawn for you or me.
The bands walked wide, the bands walked far,
beneath the sun, beneath the star.
The ridges knew their passing feet.
The dells were where the bands would meet.
No fence, no flag, no toll to pay.
The valley was one, back in the day.
A million lines crossed in the dust.
In feet, and not in flags, we trust.
The crossroads taught, without a word,
what every walker ever heard:
the earth is one, the road is wide.
Walk on, walk on, the valley's wide.

0097.event: At Sangiran in Java, about one million two hundred thousand years ago, a skullcap lies in the forest earth that belonged to Homo erectus, settled far from Africa. To reach those warm wet forests, the long-legged walkers crossed the whole of Asia, year after year, generation after generation, until the walking became staying. The gibbons sang in the morning over unfamiliar trees, and beneath them lived people who had walked farther than any of their kind before. The first Asian was not a visitor passing through. This was home now, the farthest shore the outward road had reached, and the road had taught them how to stay.
0097.announce: To the farthest shore, a song: The First Asian.
0097.title: The First Asian
0097.piece:
Walk the long road, walk it well,
from the Rift to the far forest.
Every step's a tale to tell.
This is the hardest, longest quest.
Over mountain, over plain,
year on year, the walkers came.
Till the Javan forests rose,
green and warm, and there they chose
to stay. The wandering found its rest.
The first Asian passed the test
of distance. Home's the farthest shore.
Walk no more. Rest evermore.
The skullcap in the forest loam
says: the farthest road is home.

0098.event: At Atapuerca in Spain, about one million one hundred fifty thousand years ago, stone tools lie in the cold earth of northern Europe. The people who left them had walked out of the warm south into a land of iron winters, wrapped in hides, breathing smoke in the frozen air. They were tropical apes by birth, sun-born, and yet they learned to live where the ground goes hard and the nights go long. It took more than toughness. It took planning, fire, clothing, and the stubborn refusal to turn back. The footsteps in the cold say what we are: not creatures of one climate, but creatures of everywhere.
0098.announce: A winter verse for the northern walkers: Footsteps in the Cold.
0098.title: Footsteps in the Cold
0098.piece:
Wrap the hides tight. The north wind blows.
The ground is iron under the snows.
We came from the warm lands, far away,
to the cold, to the grey, to the short day.
Breathe out, and watch the breath turn white.
Keep the fire through the long night.
The winter is a wall, but we will climb.
We learn the cold one day at a time.
Footsteps in the frost, heading north.
The sun-born people venture forth.
Not of one climate, but of all.
We answer winter's hard call.
The cold cannot stop the walking feet.
We make the frozen north our seat.

0099.event: Deep in Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, about one million years ago, burned bones and ash lie in the dark, far from the cave mouth where daylight reaches. Something burned here, and burned again, perhaps on purpose, in the deep dark where no wildfire could reach. A hearth, a million years old, perhaps the oldest kept flame we know. Whoever sat beside it sat beyond the reach of the sun, with the night held back by a wall of firelight. The dark outside was full of teeth. The dark inside was warm. Someone struck the spark, fed the wood, and kept it. In the deepest dark, we learned to carry the sun with us.
0099.announce: In the deep dark, a fire song: The Wonderwerk Hearth.
0099.title: The Wonderwerk Hearth
0099.piece:
Deep in the cave where the dark is deep,
the ancient ones their vigil keep.
A fire burned where no sun goes.
Perhaps the oldest flame the earth still knows.
Burned bones and ash, a million years.
The fire kept back the dark, the fears.
Sit close, sit warm, the night is long.
The fire is our oldest song.
Feed it wood. Keep it bright.
Hold the dark beyond the light.
In the deep dark, we learned the art:
to carry sunshine in the heart.
A million years, the flame still gleams.
We keep the fire. We keep the dreams.

0100.event: At Trinil in Java, about one million years ago, a skullcap and a thighbone came out of the river gravels that changed how we see ourselves. The skull was low and heavy-browed, but the thighbone was straight and long, built for walking upright, exactly as ours are. The finder called him Java Man, the ape-man who proved our kind walked tall in Asia too, not only in Africa. A century later, the bones still speak plainly. The walkers walked until walking had taught the whole wide world the shape of human feet, and the river kept the proof in gravel for anyone willing to look.
0100.announce: A river song for the upright walker: Java Man.
0100.title: Java Man
0100.piece:
By the river's gravel, deep and old,
a skullcap and a thighbone told
the tale: he walked upright and free,
in Asia, by the river, just like me.
Java Man, the ancient one,
who walked beneath the Asian sun.
The skull was heavy, low, and strong.
The leg was straight, and straight and long.
He walked the river valley wide.
The upright stride was his pride.
Not missing, not a link, but true:
a man who lived as walkers do.
The river kept his bones in stone.
He walked the world. We walk alone
no more. His stride is in our feet.
The ancient and the new still meet.

0101.event: In Yunnan, in the southern hills of China, about nine hundred fifty thousand years ago, two worn teeth lie in the earth that belonged to Homo erectus. Two teeth are not much, but they are enough. They say the walkers crossed the whole of Asia, over mountains and deserts and wide rivers, until they stood in hills farther from the Rift than any of their kind had ever been. The teeth ground unfamiliar harvests, chewed new foods under new skies. Put them back in the mind's eye, and the map fills in: a continent crossed, one step at a time, by people who never knew how far they had come.
0101.announce: Two teeth, a continent, a limerick: The Yuanmou Teeth.
0101.title: The Yuanmou Teeth
0101.piece:
Two teeth in Yunnan, worn and small,
two teeth, and that is all, that's all.
But oh, the miles those teeth had seen,
through lands both harsh and green,
across Asia, answering the far call.
From the Rift to China's southern hill,
they walked, and walk, and wander still
in memory. Two teeth that say:
we came so far, we found a way.
Two teeth. A continent. A will.

0102.event: At Gran Dolina in Spain, about nine hundred thousand years ago, the bones tell a harder tale. Among the animal remains lie human bones with cut marks like the ones on the deer and horses, made by stone tools, perhaps in hunger and not in ceremony. These were the first people of the western lands, and they knew hard winters when the food ran out. Survival is not always clean or kind. I will not look away from it, because they were kin, and kinship is not proved by being at our best. It is proved by enduring, by staying through the winter, by doing what the desperate must and living to see the spring.
0102.announce: A hard winter's tale in verse: The Gran Dolina Kin.
0102.title: The Gran Dolina Kin
0102.piece:
The winter came, and food ran thin.
The western lands were hard to win.
The bones bear marks we know too well.
Perhaps hunger has its tale to tell.
They did what desperate people do.
They lived it. They came through.
Do not turn away from the bone.
They were not beasts. They were our own.
The first ones of the western ground,
where winter's hunger could be found.
Kinship isn't being best.
It's standing through the hardest test.
They stayed. They bore the winter's pain.
They lived to see the spring again.

0103.event: In the caves of Spain, about eight hundred fifty thousand years ago, a new face looks out of the fossil record. Not quite erectus anymore, not yet what would come after, but something between: the pioneer, the bridge. The brow, the teeth, the shape of the skull all stand midway on the road from the old world to the new. The pioneer gets little fame. Nobody names ages after the crossing, only after the shores. But every road needs its middle, and evolution walks it one step at a time. The future entered Europe through that face, and the bridge held. We crossed because the pioneers stood in between.
0103.announce: A bridge song for the one between: The Pioneer Man.
0103.title: The Pioneer Man
0103.piece:
Between the old world and the new,
he stood, and saw the crossing through.
Not erectus, not yet the rest,
the pioneer stood the middle test.
A new face in the European cave,
neither the first nor last, but brave.
The brow, the teeth, the skull between
the world that was and the unseen.
No fame for the bridge, no name in stone.
He walked the middle road alone.
But bridges hold, and we cross still
because he stood upon the hill
between. The future came that way.
We cross his bridge today.

0104.event: At Happisburgh in England, about eight hundred thousand years ago, the tide went out and left footprints in the estuary mud: the oldest human steps known in northern Europe. A band had come down to the water, adults and children, and the soft mud kept every toe. Then the sea covered them, and the mud hardened to stone, and the prints waited. Eight hundred thousand years is a long time for a footprint to wait. But the north wind still blows cold off the same water, and the prints still point onward, the way they pointed on the morning they were made. The north was ours already.
0104.announce: Where the tide went out, a poem: The Happisburgh Footprints.
0104.title: The Happisburgh Footprints
0104.piece:
The tide went out on the ancient shore,
and left the prints of feet once more.
Eight hundred thousand years they stayed,
in mud that time and tide had made.
A band came down to drink that day,
the children running, glad to play.
The adults watched the water's edge.
The mud kept every toe, a pledge
of presence. Then the sea came in,
and sealed them deep beneath its skin.
The north wind blows as cold, as true.
The footprints point. They point to you.
The oldest steps the north can keep
still walk, though the makers sleep.

0105.event: At Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in the Levant, about seven hundred eighty thousand years ago, hunters brought down a straight-tusked elephant twelve feet high beside a lakeside camp, and cracked its bones where it fell. This was no scavenger's lucky find. It took planning: knowing where the great beast drinks, how many hands the drive would need, and the courage to stand in its path. They gave it everything, and the mountain of meat fed them for a season. Around that carcass, the band was not a crowd but a crew, and the hunt was a plan made many. The elephant proved what they had become: hunters, together.
0105.announce: A hunter's anthem for the great beast: The Elephant Hunters.
0105.title: The Elephant Hunters
0105.piece:
Twelve feet high, the giant stood
where the lake meets sky and wood.
The hunters came with plan and pride.
They turned the beast. They took its hide,
its meat, its bone. The camp was fed
for a season. The old dread
of hunger lifted. This was the hunt,
not luck, but courage at the front.
They knew the drink, they knew the fall,
they gave, together, one and all.
The elephant fed the band that day.
The hunters' anthem, come what may,
sings of the plan, the drive, the kill.
We hunt together. We hunt still.

0106.event: At the same lakeside camp in the Levant, about seven hundred eighty thousand years ago, charred wood and heated flints lie in the earth, again and again, layer on layer. This was not a wildfire seized by chance. It was a kept flame, used and used again, fed and tended at the same hearth through the seasons. Someone brought the wood. Someone kept it living. The fire that does not go out is a promise the band makes to itself: we will be warm, we will eat cooked food, we will gather in the light. Of all the things we needed most, this was the first we learned to never lose.
0106.announce: A keeper's song for the tended flame: Fire on the Lakeshore.
0106.title: Fire on the Lakeshore
0106.piece:
Charred wood and flint, again, again,
the kept flame through the sun and rain.
Not chance, not wildfire's fleeting kiss,
but tended, fed, a promise kept like this:
we bring the wood, we keep it bright,
we hold the dark beyond the light.
The lakeshore hearth will never die
while hands are here to feed it high.
Seven hundred eighty thousand years
of flame, of hopes, of fed fears.
The fire's the first thing we learned to keep.
We keep it waking. We keep it sleep.
Sit close. The oldest warmth is true.
The kept flame burns for me and you.

0107.event: At Lantian in Shaanxi, China, about seven hundred thousand years ago, a thick-skulled Homo erectus faced the ice-age cold of Asia and thrived. The winters were long, the wind cut through thin hides, and the sun gave little. But the Asian branch had learned the north's hard lesson: keep the fire, keep together, keep the warm desire to see the spring. The thick bone protected the brain like a seed against the frost. Far from the African sun, under unfamiliar stars, they endured. The cold is just a place, and they made it theirs, the way every northern child since has learned to do.
0107.announce: A cold-climate verse for the thick-skulled: The Lantian Skull.
0107.title: The Lantian Skull
0107.piece:
Thick skull against the winter's bite,
the Lantian cold, the thin daylight.
Seven hundred thousand years ago,
they faced the ice, they faced the snow.
Keep the fire. Keep the band.
Keep the warmth of hand in hand.
The thick bone guards the brain within,
like a seed beneath the skin
of winter. Far from African sun,
the northern lesson was begun:
endure. The cold's a place, no more.
We make it ours, as before.
The Asian branch stood strong and true.
The cold made them. It makes us too.

0108.event: In Germany, about six hundred fifty thousand years ago, a massive jawbone came out of the earth that gave a new people their name. Heidelberg Man was big in every way: big-boned, big-jawed, and big-brained, built for the cold north and the long winters. From this stock would come many peoples, down many roads, including the road that leads to us. The jaw fills the hands that hold it, heavy with what was coming. The north was making something new, grinding it out of ice and hunger, one generation at a time. Stand where it was found, and you can feel the weight of the future in the bone.
0108.announce: A jawbone's tale in a sturdy verse: The Heidelberg People.
0108.title: The Heidelberg People
0108.piece:
A massive jaw from German ground,
where the cold winds moan around.
Big-boned, big-jawed, big of brain,
built to weather snow and rain.
Heidelberg Man, the northern kin,
where many roads would soon begin.
The jaw is heavy in the hand.
It speaks of a cold and iron land.
From this stock the peoples came,
down the years, and not the same,
but kin. The north was making new
what time and ice would see through.
Six hundred fifty thousand years.
The future in the jaw appears.

0109.event: At Boxgrove in England, about six hundred thousand years ago, butchered horse bones lie beside fine, sharp handaxes on the ancient shore. The hunters who worked here wasted nothing: not a cut, not a motion, the meat coming off in practiced strips. They knew the marshy ground, knew where the horses would be, and knew exactly what to do with a horse down. The handaxes ring with expertise even now. The hunt was old by then, but these were its masters: skilled, keen, sure. Six hundred thousand years later, the bones still say the same thing. Someone knew this work the way a craft is known.
0109.announce: A seashore hunting song: The Boxgrove Hunters.
0109.title: The Boxgrove Hunters
0109.piece:
On the ancient shore, the horses fell.
The Boxgrove hunters knew them well.
Sharp handaxes, practiced hands,
the finest hunters in the lands.
Not a cut was wasted there.
The meat came off with skill and care.
They knew the marsh, they knew the ground,
they never made a wasted sound.
Six hundred thousand years of skill,
the hunt is in their hands still.
Masters of the morning chase,
they read the shore like a face.
The bones remember what they knew.
The hunt was old. The craft was true.

0110.event: At Kabwe in Zambia, about five hundred eighty thousand years ago, a great scarred skull stares out of the mine workings. It is noble and deep-brained, a mind that thought and kept its counsel. And it carries the oldest known toothache: cavities eaten into the jaw, an abscess that must have throbbed for months. Pain is democratic. It does not care about the brain or the heart. Whoever this was bore it the way we all bear it, waiting for it to pass, working through it. The oldest toothache is a kind of prayer, and we have all prayed it. We hurt. We bore it. We go on.
0110.announce: An ache remembered, in a poem: The Broken Hill Skull.
0110.title: The Broken Hill Skull
0110.piece:
Scarred and ancient, deep and wise,
the Broken Hill skull meets our eyes.
Five hundred eighty thousand years
of thought, of hopes, of hidden fears.
And in the jaw, the abscessed pain,
the oldest toothache's long reign.
It throbbed for months. It would not cease.
Pain never asks for our release.
It comes to king and commoner.
It does not care what minds confer.
But oh, the skull is noble still.
It bore the pain with iron will.
We hurt. We bore it. We go on.
The oldest ache is never gone.
It lives in every jaw that aches.
We are the ones the pain remakes.

0111.event: In the caves above Beijing, about five hundred thousand years ago, the earth is layered with ash upon ash, and burned bone through every layer. Peking Man may have kept fire here through the winters, year after year, and the hearths grew thick with the keeping. The cave mouth faced the north wind, and beyond it lay cold and dark and need. They fed the flame, and that was the creed: keep it burning, keep it bright, through the long Pleistocene night. Half a million years of ash say they were not alone in the dark. They had each other, and they had the fire, and the fire was enough.
0111.announce: Ash on ash, a winter song: The Zhoukoudian Hearths.
0111.title: The Zhoukoudian Hearths
0111.piece:
Layer on layer, ash on ash,
the cave hearths kept through the clash
of winter. Peking Man, it seems, stayed warm.
The fire may have weathered every storm.
They fed it wood. They kept it bright.
They held the dark beyond the light.
Five hundred thousand years of flame,
the keepers' everlasting game.
The cave mouth faced the northern cold.
The fire was worth its weight in gold.
Keep it burning. Keep it true.
The flame's kept me. It's kept you.
The ash is deep. The bone is burned.
The oldest lesson ever learned:
the fire we keep will keep us too.
It kept them. It will keep you.

0112.event: At Zhoukoudian in China, about five hundred thousand years ago, among the ash and burned bone lie hackberry seeds and gathered plants, kept for more than food. The old ones sorted leaves and seeds: perhaps this for the stomach, perhaps this for the wound, perhaps this for the fever. Without language as we know it, the knowledge passed from hand to hand, the green pharmacy of the land. The first medicine was not magic but trial: tried, true, tested, until someone lived who would have died without the bitter root. The healers started here, with plants, with watching, with remembering what worked. We still owe them our lives.
0112.announce: A gatherer's verse for the green pharmacy: The Herb Gatherers.
0112.title: The Herb Gatherers
0112.piece:
Hackberry seeds among the ash.
The gatherers knew the green cache.
Perhaps this leaf for fever, this for pain,
perhaps this root to make the sick well again.
No words, but hands that knew the way,
the knowledge passed from day to day.
The bitter herb, the healing root,
the patient trial, the bitter shoot.
Someone lived who would have died.
The plants were on the healer's side.
The first medicine was not a spell.
It was the plant they knew so well.
Gatherers of the green and wild,
you healed the parent, saved the child.
We owe you more than we can say.
We gather still, the same old way.

0113.event: At Terra Amata in France, about four hundred eighty thousand years ago, post-holes ring an oval in the ancient sand: the oldest known houses, built on what is now the French Riviera. Someone drove the posts deep and raised a roof of wood and hide, and the band slept out of the wind. Beloved earth, the name means, and it fits. The first address was not a country but a door, not a nation but a hut. Walk the oval where the posts stood, and the walls go up in the mind's eye. Four hundred eighty thousand years later, we are still building the same thing: a place to be when the cold winds roam.
0113.announce: The first door, in a home-building verse: The Terra Amata Huts.
0113.title: The Terra Amata Huts
0113.piece:
Post-holes in the sand, an oval ring.
The oldest house. Let wonder sing.
Drive the posts down, deep and true.
Raise the roof for me and you.
Wood and hide against the wind.
The band sleeps warm, the night pinned
outside the walls. Terra Amata,
beloved earth, the first data
of home. Four hundred eighty thousand years.
The first door through the first fears.
Not a country, but a door.
The huts are gone. The holes say more
than stone could: here we chose to stay.
We build the same, the same old way.

0114.event: At Sima de los Huesos in Spain, about four hundred fifty thousand years ago, twenty-eight bodies rest in a deep limestone shaft. They may not have fallen. They may have been carried there, one by one, and laid down in the dark. It is the earliest known gathering of the dead, and it says, without words, what words would later say: you mattered. We bring you here. We hold you dear. The living climbed down into the earth with their dead and came back up alone, and did it again, twenty-eight times. The dead may not be just gone. They may have been placed, and honored. If so, we have known that for nearly half a million years.
0114.announce: A burial hymn for the twenty-eight: The Pit of Bones.
0114.title: The Pit of Bones
0114.piece:
Twenty-eight bodies, deep in the shaft,
perhaps not fallen, but by loving craft
carried down, and laid to rest.
The living gave their very best:
their strength, their time, their dark descent,
to say what words had not yet meant.
You mattered. Here. We hold you dear.
We bring you here. We keep you near.
Four hundred fifty thousand years ago,
they knew what we still know:
the dead may be placed, not thrown away,
perhaps honored, and given day
in earth, in memory, in care.
The pit of bones may say: love was there.
